summary: In Greek mythology, Anius (Ancient Greek Ἄνιος) is king of Delos and priest of Apollo, son of Apollo and Rhoeo. He hosts Aeneas on the flight from Troy and is father of the Oenotropae — daughters granted by Dionysus the power to produce wine, grain, and oil — whom Agamemnon tries to seize for the Achaean army.

sections.heading: Priest-king of Delos
paragraphs: Rhoeo, daughter of Staphylus, bears Apollo's child; exposed in a chest, she reaches Delos or Euboea and places the infant on Apollo's altar. Apollo rears Anius in prophecy; he becomes the god's priest and king of Delos. By Dorippe he has three daughters — Oeno, Spermo, and Elais (the Wine-growers / Oenotropae) — and sons including the eponyms Andros and Mykonos.

When the Greeks touch at Delos en route to Troy, Anius prophesies a ten-year war and offers his daughters' magical provisions for nine years. Agamemnon tries to take the Oenotropae by force; they pray to Dionysus and are changed into doves (Ovid; Apollodorus' Epitome). Virgil and Ovid later show aged Anius receiving Anchises and Aeneas as a guest-friend on Apollo's isle.

sections.heading: Homonym note
paragraphs: Anius is this Delian priest-king alone. A rare Roman strand marries a prophetic daughter Lavinia/Launa to Aeneas — not to be confused with Latinus' Lavinia of the Aeneid's Italian books.
